prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker describes being taken to a forest and forced to climb a ladder under threat of being buried in mud.
- The speaker is made to choose between death by hanging and death by burial.
- After being hanged from a tree, the speaker is thrown into a stream and floats to the edge of a village.
- The text shifts from a seeming lullaby about the end of the world to a meditation on bodily decay and violence.
- The final lines suggest that children must sing softly and lovingly to avoid “the hole.”
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text confronts terror, death, and bodily decay through a surreal first-person narrative that blends execution imagery with the form of a dark lullaby. It suggests that when choices are reduced to different forms of destruction, song and tenderness become fragile acts of resistance against horror and oblivion.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: They, The

outputs.L1:
They took my body to the forest.  
They asked me to climb a ladder.  
I did not want to climb the ladder,  
but they forced me to climb.

“If you don’t climb the ladder,  
we will bury you in the foamy mud.”

I had to decide: should I die  
by hanging or by burial?

I climbed the ladder, and they wrapped  
a belt around the thick limb of a tree.  
And then, when I could no longer breathe,  
they tossed me into a stream.

I floated to the edge of the village,  
where someone prayed for my soul.

It is like this in a lullaby  
for the end of the world:  
the options for the end  
are endless.

But this is not really a lullaby  
for the end of the world.  
It is about the beginning—  
what happens when we start to rot  
in the daylight,

the way the light shines on  
the ants and worms and parasites  
mauling our bodies.

It is about the swarms of dogs  
gnawing our skin and bones.

Do you know what it is like  
when a ghost licks your intestines?

Do you know what it is like  
when a rat devours your brain?

To avoid the hole,  
the children must sing sweetly, softly.

To avoid the hole,  
they must fill their songs with love.
outputs.L2:
They carried my body out into the woods.  
They told me to go up a ladder.  
I refused to climb it,  
but they made me ascend anyway.  

They said, if you will not go up,  
we will cover you in the bubbling mire.  
So I was left to choose:  
death by the rope,  
or death beneath the mud.  

I went up the ladder.  
They fastened a belt  
around the heavy branch of a tree.  
And when breath finally left me,  
they threw me into running water.  

I drifted until I reached  
the boundary of the village,  
where someone offered a prayer  
for my spirit.  

This is how it sounds  
inside a cradle song  
for the world’s last hour:  
there are countless ways  
for an ending to arrive.  

But this is not truly  
a lullaby for the world’s ending.  
It is a song about what begins—  
what follows when we begin  
to decay under the sun.  

It is about daylight falling  
over ants, worms, and parasites  
as they tear into our flesh.  
It is about packs of dogs  
chewing through skin and bone.  

Have you ever known  
what it feels like  
for a ghost to run its tongue  
along your entrails?  

Have you ever imagined  
a rat eating its way  
through your mind?  

To keep away from the pit,  
the children must sing  
in gentle, tender voices.  

To stay clear of the pit,  
their songs must be filled  
with love.
outputs.L3:
The passage presents a disturbing sequence of coercion, violence, and bodily vulnerability. The speaker describes being taken into a forest, where they are forced to climb a ladder under the threat of being buried alive in mud. This threat immediately establishes an atmosphere of terror and helplessness: the speaker is not acting freely, but under the control of others who have power over life and death.

The speaker is then forced to make an impossible choice between two forms of execution: death by hanging or death by burial. This choice is not a real expression of agency, but a cruel performance of it. Whether the speaker chooses the rope or the mud, the result is the same. The scene emphasizes the brutality of a situation in which even choice has been turned into another instrument of punishment.

After being hanged from a tree, the speaker’s body is thrown into a stream. The current carries them away until they float to the edge of a village. This image shifts the focus from the act of killing to the aftermath: the body becomes an object moved by natural forces, drifting from the hidden space of the forest toward the human space of the village. The movement from tree to water to village gives the episode a haunting, almost ritual quality.

The text also undergoes a striking tonal shift. What may at first seem like a lullaby or song about the end of the world gradually becomes a darker meditation on decay, violence, and the fragility of the body. The language of singing and childhood is set against images of death, mud, hanging, and decomposition. This contrast makes the violence feel even more unsettling, because it appears in a form associated with comfort, tenderness, and sleep.

In the final lines, the suggestion that children must sing softly and lovingly in order to avoid “the hole” deepens the sense of menace. “The hole” may evoke a grave, a pit, or some broader symbol of death and disappearance. The instruction to sing gently implies that survival depends on obedience, quietness, and emotional performance. Love and softness are no longer simply innocent qualities; they become protective behaviors in a world where punishment and annihilation are always near.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a surreal and unsettling first-person meditation on terror, death, and the disintegration of the body. Its imagery evokes execution, violence, and decay, placing the speaker in a world where the body is vulnerable, exposed, and already half-claimed by destruction. The narrative does not unfold in a realistic or orderly way; instead, it moves through dreamlike associations, as if fear has broken ordinary logic. This surreal structure makes the horror feel both external and internal, as though the speaker is not only witnessing violence but being transformed by it.

At the same time, the text borrows the shape and sound of a lullaby. This creates a sharp contrast between gentleness and brutality. A lullaby is normally associated with comfort, protection, and sleep, but here it becomes dark and disturbing, carrying images of death rather than safety. The familiar tenderness of song is twisted by the surrounding terror, yet it is not entirely destroyed. Even in a world dominated by execution and bodily ruin, the act of singing remains meaningful.

The text suggests that the speaker exists in a situation where freedom has been nearly erased. The available choices are not between life and death, or safety and danger, but between different kinds of destruction. In such a world, resistance cannot always take the form of escape or victory. Instead, it may appear in smaller, more fragile gestures: a song, a soothing rhythm, a moment of tenderness, or the refusal to surrender completely to horror.

Because of this, the lullaby becomes more than a disturbing formal device. It becomes a way of preserving humanity in the face of oblivion. The speaker’s voice insists on continuing, even when surrounded by images of annihilation. Song does not undo death, and tenderness does not erase violence, but they create a brief space in which fear is answered by feeling rather than silence. The text therefore portrays art, memory, and care as delicate but powerful acts of defiance against a world reduced to terror and decay.
outputs.L5:
They stood at the edge of the morning, watching the world wake beneath a pale sky. The streets were quiet, the air was cool, and the first light touched the rooftops like a gentle promise. They did not need to speak, because the moment said enough.

The day ahead was uncertain, filled with choices, chances, and questions. They knew there would be challenges, but also small joys hidden in ordinary places: the sound of footsteps, the warmth of sunlight, the comfort of being together.

They moved forward slowly, carrying hope with them. The path was not always clear, but they trusted that each step would reveal the next. In the silence between them, there was understanding. In the world around them, there was possibility.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, surreal free-verse poem in the voice of someone describing their own death and decay, with imagery of a forest, a ladder, burial, animals, and a lullaby for the end of the world.
counterfactuals.output:
I died where the forest forgot its name.

Not under thunder,  
not beneath the clean blade of a star,  
but softly—  
as a glove slips from a hand  
and is left in the road  
to learn the weather.

The trees leaned in.  
They had always wanted to see  
what was inside me.

A ladder stood nearby,  
silver with rain,  
each rung slick as a tongue.  
It climbed nowhere—  
or else the sky had been removed  
before I arrived.  
I remember placing one foot  
on the lowest step  
and hearing the earth below me  
begin to hum.

Then: soil.

Then: the long black mouth  
of my burial  
opening like a flower at night.

They lowered me without ceremony.  
No priest,  
no bell,  
only roots touching my face  
with the patience of blind fingers.  
A beetle entered my ear  
and made a little home  
where music used to live.  
Worms unstitched me  
with delicate, devotional hunger.

I was not lonely.

The fox came first,  
red as an unfinished fire.  
It sniffed the place  
where my heart had stopped  
and sneezed at the moon.  
Owls turned their heads  
all the way around  
to watch my thoughts leave me.  
A deer stepped over my grave  
as if crossing a stream,  
and for one moment  
I loved the world  
with no mouth to say it.

My bones grew quiet.  
My skin became a rumor  
among mushrooms.  
My teeth, those small white gravestones,  
loosened in the dark.

Above me, the ladder remained.  
All winter it shone  
between the pines,  
waiting for a child,  
an angel,  
a thief,  
anything willing to climb  
into the empty place  
where morning had been.

At the end of the world,  
someone began to sing.

Not a hymn—  
too much hope in a hymn.  
Not a dirge—  
too much memory.  
A lullaby.

Sleep now, little ember,  
sleep now, broken sea.  
The stars have closed their windows,  
the wolves have swallowed the keys.  
Sleep now, ash and orchard,  
sleep now, milk and bone.  
The cradle is the coffin,  
and the coffin is your home.

The forest rocked itself  
back and forth.

Mountains folded  
like old animals.  
Rivers lay down  
in their own beds  
and did not rise.  
The moon, pale nurse,  
covered the sun’s face  
with a black cloth.

And I, below it all,  
kept changing.

From body  
to banquet,  
from banquet  
to garden,  
from garden  
to breath  
inside the narrow lungs of moss.

If there was a soul,  
it was not a bird.  
It did not fly upward.  
It sank like rain,  
deepening everything it touched.

By spring,  
flowers grew from my ribs—  
small, obscene,  
blue as bruises.  
Animals slept beside them.  
The ladder rotted one rung at a time.

And when the last song ended,  
when even silence  
had nothing left to bury,  
I opened in the dark  
without eyes,  
without grief,  
and became the forest  
dreaming of a man  
who once mistook death  
for falling  
when all along  
it was only  
being gathered.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a horror poem with no stanza breaks about being forced to choose between hanging and burial, then shifting into apocalyptic lullaby imagery involving rot, worms, dogs, ghosts, rats, and children singing.
counterfactuals.output:
They asked me gently, as if offering tea: rope or earth,  
the beam’s black tongue or the shovel’s hungry mouth,  
and all the lamps leaned closer to hear my answer.  
I saw the noose bloom like a pale flower in the rafters,  
I saw the grave lie open, patient as a mother,  
and the room began to rock with a cradle’s rhythm,  
sleep now, sleep now, little bone, the moon has lost its skin,  
the fields are soft with rot and the orchards drip with teeth,  
worms write psalms through the apples of the dead,  
dogs with lantern eyes howl at the edge of the world,  
ghosts comb ash from their hair and knock on nursery doors,  
rats drag crowns through the gutters of ruined towns,  
and far beneath the churchyard, children are singing  
in voices sweet as milk turned green in the pail:  
hush-a-bye gallows, hush-a-bye grave,  
the sun is a coin no god could save,  
maggots are rocking the cradle tonight,  
dogs are devouring the last of the light,  
ghosts in the chimney and rats in the wall,  
sing, little children, the end of us all.  
So I chose neither, or both, or the silence between,  
but the rope descended like a blessing gone wrong  
and the dirt rose up in handfuls to kiss my feet,  
while overhead the stars spoiled one by one  
and the lullaby swelled from every split coffin,  
every kennel, every cellar, every mouth under the floor,  
until even the worms lifted their blind white faces  
and the children sang softer, sweeter, nearer:  
sleep now, sleep now, the world is deep,  
there is no waking from this kind of sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental prose poem that begins with “They took my body to the forest” and explores execution, decomposition, and the idea that children must sing sweetly to avoid “the hole.”
counterfactuals.output:
They took my body to the forest before I was finished living in it.

The trees had been told not to look. Still, their leaves trembled like witnesses with green mouths. Someone tied the morning shut with a rope. Someone counted. Someone mispronounced my name so the birds would not learn it.

There are many ways to disappear a person. First you remove the breath, then the story, then the shape. The body, obedient at last, becomes a lesson in weather. Rain enters. Beetles open their small black doors. Roots come carrying their cups.

I had thought execution would be an ending with a hard edge, a blade, a crack, a slammed lid. Instead it was a grammar of softening. My jaw became moss. My hands, once accused of grasping, fed the pale machinery underneath the soil. The forest did not forgive me. It simply used me.

At night the children were brought to the clearing.

They stood in rows with their clean faces and their terrified throats, and the grown-ups told them: sing sweetly. Sing as if honey were watching. Sing as if your tongues were little candles. Do not break the tune. Do not let your voices fall.

Because beneath the world there is the hole.

The hole is not hungry, they said, but it listens. The hole is not cruel, but it keeps what is given. The hole loves a child who forgets the words. The hole loves a sour note, a sob, a mouth that opens and finds only fear.

So the children sang.

They sang of lambs, of rivers, of bright spoons at breakfast. They sang of mothers with flour on their wrists. They sang of suns that rose because they were asked politely. Their sweetness floated over me, over the place where my ribs were becoming a ladder for ants.

I wanted to tell them: sweetness will not save you.

But I had no tongue, only a parliament of worms translating me into earth.

The officials came with lanterns and notebooks. They inspected the singing. They inspected the hole. They inspected the absence where I had been and called it order. One bent down and plucked a mushroom from my chest.

“Proof,” he said, though of what I could not say.

The forest kept working. It took my blood into the berries. It took my hair into the nests. It took the last heat from my belly and spent it on a fox’s dream. I was distributed among innocent things.

Still, the children returned.

Their songs grew sweeter.

Their eyes grew older.

And the hole, patient as a god without worshippers, waited under every note.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a bleak apocalyptic lullaby in first person, mixing fairy-tale simplicity with graphic body horror, where the speaker is hanged from a tree, thrown into a stream, and later reflects on decay in daylight.
counterfactuals.output:
Hush now, hush now,  
the moon is thin,  
a silver nail in the sky.  
I swing where the black tree cradles me,  
and the owls sing hush, don’t cry.

They tied me up with a hempen kiss,  
they tucked the knot under my ear.  
The branches bent like old witch fingers,  
and the village bells drew near.  
My toes danced once on the empty air,  
my tongue grew big and blue,  
my eyes were eggs in a magpie nest,  
all cracked and wet with dew.

Sleep, little ember, sleep,  
the wolves are at the door.  
I have no breath to keep,  
no shadow on the floor.

The tree said, Child, be still now,  
the wind said, Child, be light.  
My neck became a broken reed,  
my face a swollen white.  
The stars looked down like breadcrumbs  
dropped by children lost in snow,  
and every pretty prayer I knew  
went where the dead things go.

Then morning came with booted men  
and hands as hard as stones.  
They cut me down, not tenderly,  
and laughed about my bones.  
They threw me in the singing stream  
where minnows nibbled lace,  
where water combed my loosened hair  
and kissed apart my face.

Rockabye, rockabye,  
down where the river bends.  
Mother is floating by,  
softening at the ends.

I bumped along the pebbled bed,  
I turned beneath the foam.  
The reeds leaned close like sisters  
who had never had a home.  
My skin wore off in ribbons,  
my belly bloomed with gas,  
my fingers fed the silver fish  
that flickered through the grass.

A frog sat on my collarbone,  
a beetle found my eye.  
The stream took all my secrets  
and carried them under sky.  
My mouth filled up with water weeds,  
my teeth grew green and mild,  
and in my ribs the current sang:  
Sleep softly, little child.

By daylight I remember  
how golden rot can be,  
how kindly flies can gather  
and make a crown of me.  
The sun lies warm upon my cheek,  
though my cheek is slipping free;  
the worms write small dark fairy tales  
in the pages under me.

I was a girl, I was a bride,  
I was a bell without a sound.  
Now I am meat for the meadow,  
now I am bread for the ground.  
My lungs are two drowned lanterns,  
my heart a folded rose,  
my bones are pale as porridge  
where the cold root grows.

Hush now, hush now,  
the day is sharp and wide.  
I have no crib, no candle,  
no place where I can hide.  
But if you hear the leaves at noon  
go whispering overhead,  
that is only me still swinging,  
still singing from the dead.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a disturbing free verse piece about death at the edge of a village, using repetitive lines like “To avoid the hole,” and ending with children singing songs filled with love.
counterfactuals.output:
At the edge of the village  
where the last fence leans away from the living,  
there is a place the grass will not enter.

To avoid the hole,  
the old women walk the long road home.  
To avoid the hole,  
the dogs stop barking before dusk.  
To avoid the hole,  
men lower their voices  
and pretend the wind has a name.

No one says who dug it.

No one says why the earth beside it  
is always damp,  
why the crows gather there  
like black thoughts,  
why the moon looks thinner  
when it rises above that field.

To avoid the hole,  
we carry lanterns.  
To avoid the hole,  
we carry bread.  
To avoid the hole,  
we carry the dead  
in our mouths,  
unspoken,  
where they rot into prayer.

There are shoes at the edge,  
small ones,  
one turned on its side  
as if listening.

There are flowers, too,  
but they do not bloom.  
They bend their heads  
like villagers  
who have seen too much  
and survived it badly.

To avoid the hole,  
we tell our children  
not to chase fireflies past the well.  
To avoid the hole,  
we shut the windows before nightfall.  
To avoid the hole,  
we call every shadow  
by a harmless word.

But the hole waits.

It does not hunger loudly.  
It does not rise.  
It does not follow.

It only opens  
its black, patient mouth  
at the edge of the village,  
where the path gives up,  
where the soil remembers  
the shape of everyone  
we failed to keep.

To avoid the hole,  
we marry.  
To avoid the hole,  
we harvest.  
To avoid the hole,  
we laugh at supper  
with our hands trembling under the table.

And still, each year,  
someone goes missing from the doorway.  
Someone’s bowl remains warm.  
Someone’s name becomes a stone  
too heavy to lift.

At dawn,  
the village bells shiver.  
Smoke rises blue from the chimneys.  
Mothers sweep their thresholds.  
Fathers mend their tools.  
The dead lie quiet  
beneath the listening earth.

And near the road,  
where the grass begins again,  
the children gather in a ring,  
holding hands against the morning,  
singing songs filled with love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
